ai.title: Aortic Regurgitation
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Aortic regurgitation is a back‑flow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole, leading to volume overload and eventual heart failure. It is common in low‑resource settings due to rheumatic fever and infections.

sections.p: Aortic regurgitation (AR) is diastolic back‑flow across a diseased aortic valve. Diagnosis relies on history, exam, and simple investigations available in low‑resource hospitals.
b: Early diastolic decrescendo murmur at left sternal border

t.b: Shows wide pulse pressure; >60 mmHg difference suggests significant AR
Confirms valve morphology, regurgitant fraction, LV size; if unavailable, use Doppler of carotid pulse
Shows enlarged cardiac silhouette, pulmonary venous congestion if left‑sided failure
May show left ventricular hypertrophy or atrial enlargement

sections.p: Severity is graded by regurgitant fraction and LV response. The most used system is the American Heart Association (AHA) stages A–D.
b: Stage A: asymptomatic, mild regurgitation, normal LV size
Stage B: asymptomatic, moderate regurgitation, LV dilation
Stage C: symptomatic, severe regurgitation, LV dysfunction
Stage D: refractory heart failure, end‑stage

sections.p: In East Africa, rheumatic heart disease and infections dominate. Other causes include congenital bicuspid valve, syphilis, and trauma.

t.b: Positive treponemal test indicates syphilitic aortitis
History of untreated sore throat suggests rheumatic fever

sections.p: Patients often report exertional dyspnea, palpitations, and a feeling of rapid heartbeats. Physical signs include a high‑pitched early diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure.

t.b: Detects early diastolic murmur; absence of murmur does not rule out AR
Water‑hammer pulse indicates high stroke volume and low diastolic pressure

sections.p: Use the simplest tests first; if unavailable, rely on clinical judgment.

t.b: Wide pulse pressure (>60 mmHg) suggests significant AR
Left ventricular hypertrophy or atrial enlargement may be present
Cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion indicates advanced disease
Gold standard; shows valve morphology, regurgitant fraction, LV size and function

sections.p: Urgent care is needed if signs of acute decompensation or endocarditis appear.

t.b: Positive in infective endocarditis; guides antibiotic choice
Detects vegetations or rapid valve destruction

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control volume overload, and monitor LV function. Surgery is definitive but often unavailable.
b: Beta‑blockers to reduce heart rate and improve diastolic filling
ACE inhibitors or ARBs for LV remodeling

t.b: Reduces heart rate, increases diastolic time, lowers LV filling pressure
Improves LV remodeling; avoid if renal dysfunction

sections.p: Regular monitoring of LV size and function is essential. Prevention focuses on rheumatic fever control and infection management.

t.b: Detects progression; repeat every 6–12 months in moderate cases

sections.p: Other causes of wide pulse pressure and diastolic murmurs can mimic AR.
b: Mitral regurgitation (high‑pitched early diastolic murmur, but heard best at apex)

sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal early in disease or be affected by comorbidities.
b: Normal chest X‑ray in early disease
Echocardiography may underestimate regurgitant fraction if Doppler angle is poor

faq.q: What is the most common cause of AR in East Africa?
faq.a: Rheumatic heart disease due to untreated streptococcal pharyngitis.

faq.q: How do you differentiate AR from mitral regurgitation on exam?
faq.a: AR murmur is early diastolic, heard best at left sternal border; MR is early diastolic, best at apex.

faq.q: Why are beta‑blockers preferred in AR?
faq.a: They slow the heart, increasing diastolic filling time and reducing regurgitant volume.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a patient with suspected AR in a low‑resource setting? — Blood pressure to assess pulse pressure, then ECG, chest X‑ray, and echocardiography if available.
A patient with AR presents with exertional dyspnea and a high‑pitched diastolic murmur. Which sign is most specific for AR? — Wide pulse pressure (water‑hammer pulse).
You suspect infective endocarditis in a patient with AR. Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate? — Penicillin G plus gentamicin for streptococcal endocarditis.

A 45‑year‑old patient with AR has a sudden drop in blood pressure and pulmonary oedema. What is the most urgent management step? — Immediate diuretics and vasodilators to reduce preload and afterload.
Which pharmacologic agent is contraindicated in AR with renal dysfunction? — ACE inhibitors (risk of hyperkalaemia and worsening renal function).
A patient with AR has a normal ECG and chest X‑ray. What is the next best step to confirm severity? — Echocardiography to quantify regurgitant fraction and LV size.
